findings.claim: Every practice question in all ten lessons is labelled with another board's form: '2 marks - Describe One Feature', '4 marks - Describe Two Features', '8 marks - Explain Causation', '16 marks - Significance Question', '5 marks - Historic Environment Explain', '18 marks - Depth Study Essay'.
findings.truth: This paper has four question slots only. The British depth study is examined by an 'Explain...' question worth 10 marks and an essay using sources worth 20 marks, with 5 further marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar. The study of the historic environment is examined by an 'Explain...' question worth 10 marks and a source comparison worth 10 marks, with no SPaG marks. There is no describe, significance, interpretation or 18-mark form. All 60 labels relabelled, and the mark schemes that named a wrong tariff rewritten.
findings.evidence: specs/ocr/history-a-J410.md: British depth study assessment table and study of the historic environment assessment table (component group 3); paper totals 55 marks in 1 hour 15 minutes

findings.claim: Eighteen questions carry the stimulus rubric 'You may use the following in your answer: X; Y. You must also use information of your own.'
findings.truth: That bullet-stimulus rubric belongs to a different board. This paper's Explain question is set without a stimulus list. The rubric was removed from every stem.
findings.evidence: specs/ocr/history-a-J410.md, component group 3 assessment tables (the questions are 'Explain ...' and 'Essay using sources ...')

findings.claim: A '2 marks - Describe One Feature' answer that names a feature and adds one specific detail will score full marks.
findings.truth: No describe question exists on this paper. Rewritten to say that both depth-study questions need explanation, keeping the vocabulary advice.
findings.evidence: specs/ocr/history-a-J410.md, British depth study assessment table

findings.claim: Naming specific architectural features and their approximate dates earns the second mark in a 'describe one feature' question.
findings.truth: The historic environment section sets an Explain question (10 marks) and a source comparison (10 marks). Rewritten to the explain form, keeping the advice about naming phases and dates.
findings.evidence: specs/ocr/history-a-J410.md, study of the historic environment assessment table

findings.claim: 'The exam rewards students who can hold both views' (Duffy against Dickens) and 'For this exam, the key skill is using evidence to support whichever interpretation a question presents'.
findings.truth: No AO4 marks are available on this paper; interpretations are examined in the period study, not here. Both sentences rewritten so the historiography stays as background but is not presented as assessed.
findings.evidence: specs/ocr/history-a-J410.md, component group 3 tables (AO1, AO2 and AO3 only)

findings.claim: Thomas More resigned as Lord Chancellor in 1532 over the Submission of the Clergy, refusing to take the oath required by the succession legislation.
findings.truth: More resigned on 16 May 1532, the day after the Submission of the Clergy. The Act of Succession and its oath came in 1534; he refused the oath in April 1534 and was then imprisoned. The sentence made a 1532 resignation depend on a statute that did not yet exist.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Thomas More' and 'Submission of the Clergy'

findings.claim: He also confirmed the validity of Henry's secret marriage to Anne Boleyn, who had already been crowned queen.
findings.truth: Cranmer declared the Catherine marriage void on 23 May 1533 and confirmed the Anne marriage on 28 May 1533. Anne was crowned on 1 June 1533, after both rulings, not before.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Anne Boleyn' and 'Thomas Cranmer'

findings.claim: Questions on the Reformation Parliament often ask whether the break with Rome was religious or political.
findings.truth: The specification states that learners are not required to know the break with Rome and its international politics except as background. The named content is Henry's desire to annul his first marriage and the legislation of the Reformation Parliament 1529-1534. Reworded so students revise the legislation, not the diplomacy.
findings.evidence: specs/ocr/history-a-J410.md, 'The English Reformation c.1520-c.1550' scope note and key topic content

findings.claim: The Pilgrimage of Grace began in Lincolnshire in October 1536 and spread rapidly to Yorkshire and the north.
findings.truth: The specification names two risings: the Lincolnshire Rising and the Pilgrimage of Grace. The Lincolnshire Rising began at Louth on 1 October 1536; the Pilgrimage of Grace broke out separately in Yorkshire under Robert Aske days later.
findings.evidence: specs/ocr/history-a-J410.md, Dissolution key topic content ('the Lincolnshire Rising and the Pilgrimage of Grace 1536-1537'); Wikipedia 'Pilgrimage of Grace'

findings.claim: 'signals to the examiner that you know primary-source level detail'; 'impresses examiners' (lesson 7); 'the exam rewards those who can link specific legislation to specific moments' (lesson 6).
findings.truth: Invented claims about examiner reactions. Rewritten as statements about the answer itself, keeping the same advice.
findings.evidence: house rule on fabricated examiner claims

findings.claim: The Great Mere was created 'in the 1240s' and 'c.1244' by the castle's owners, repeated in the key fact, the takeaways, a flashcard, the glossary and again in lesson 9.
findings.truth: King John created the water defences between 1210 and 1216, damming the Finham and Inchford brooks to form the Great Mere. The date matters: the mere was already two generations old when it defeated the besiegers in 1266.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Kenilworth Castle' (King John spent 1,115 pounds on the castle 1210-1216 and dammed the brooks to create the Great Mere)

findings.claim: Its walls are up to 4.5 metres thick (Caesar's Tower), repeated in a knowledge check stem and a flashcard.
findings.truth: The great tower's walls are about 5 metres (16 feet) thick.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Kenilworth Castle'

findings.claim: Leicester also created a tiltyard, an elaborate garden and a gatehouse lodge on the northern approach.
findings.truth: The tiltyard ran along the dam and was already there; Leicester's father, John Dudley, widened it before 1553. Leicester built the gatehouse and laid out the garden.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Kenilworth Castle'

findings.claim: In 1244 Henry III took formal possession of the castle, recognising its strategic importance in the centre of England. Repeated as a knowledge check match pair.
findings.truth: In 1244 Henry III granted Kenilworth to Simon de Montfort, 6th Earl of Leicester. He gave it away rather than taking it, and that grant is what put the castle in rebel hands for the 1266 siege.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Kenilworth Castle'

findings.claim: After the defeat of Simon de Montfort the Younger at Evesham in 1265, his supporters retreated to Kenilworth. A flashcard answers 'Who held the castle against Henry III in the 1266 siege?' with 'Simon de Montfort the Younger'.
findings.truth: The elder Simon de Montfort, 6th Earl of Leicester, was defeated and killed at Evesham on 4 August 1265. His son was beaten at Kenilworth on 1 August 1265, was not at Evesham, and had left for France before the siege opened on 21 June 1266. The garrison was commanded by Henry de Hastings.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Kenilworth Castle' (Henry de Hastings commanded the rebels; siege 21 June to 14 December 1266) and 'Battle of Evesham'

findings.claim: The entertainment included theatrical performances (including an early adaptation of a Lancelot story).
findings.truth: No Lancelot play is recorded at Kenilworth in 1575. The recorded entertainments were pageants, fireworks, bear baiting, hunting, banquets and a play staged by men from Coventry.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Kenilworth Castle', 1575 visit

findings.claim: Kenilworth Priory (an Augustinian house that survived until 1538).
findings.truth: The Augustinian house founded by Geoffrey de Clinton in 1119 was raised to abbey status in 1447. In 1535 the Valor recorded St Mary's Abbey, Kenilworth; it was surrendered on 15 April 1538.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Kenilworth Abbey'

findings.claim: The historic environment paper tests a specific skill.
findings.truth: The historic environment is a section of the depth-study paper, not a paper of its own.
findings.evidence: specs/ocr/history-a-J410.md, component group 3 assessment

findings.claim: Lessons 1, 2, 5 and 7 teach named historians (Duffy, Dickens, Haigh, Bernard, Scarisbrick, MacCulloch) and, before this pass, set two practice questions per lesson on the significance of a historian's argument.
findings.truth: Two defensible readings. (a) Keep the historiography: it gives students the balanced-judgement material the 20-mark essay needs, and F5 has already removed the claim that it is assessed. (b) Cut it back: none of it is examined, and it costs revision time on a 12-hour depth study. Recommendation: keep it, because the essay rewards weighing evidence, but never reintroduce a practice question that asks about a historian rather than about the period.
findings.evidence: specs/ocr/history-a-J410.md, component group 3 tables (no AO4 marks)

findings.claim: A knowledge check and a flashcard drill Kett's Rebellion 1549 (Norfolk, enclosure), which this option's content list does not name.
findings.truth: The named risings for this option are the Lincolnshire Rising, the Pilgrimage of Grace 1536-1537 and the Prayer Book Rebellion 1549. Kett's Rebellion is in period and is the natural contrast that shows the western rising was religious. Recommendation: keep it, because the contrast is what makes the causation argument work, but Tom may prefer to fold it into the Prayer Book Rebellion item rather than drill it as free-standing recall.
findings.evidence: specs/ocr/history-a-J410.md, 'The impact of the Reformation in English parishes c.1534-c.1550' content

findings.claim: The survey found that the monasteries collectively had an annual income of around 165,000 pounds, repeated in a key fact, a takeaway, a knowledge check answer and a flashcard.
findings.truth: 165,000 pounds is the gross figure usually given; the net figure in the Valor is nearer 136,000 pounds, and many textbooks round to 160,000 pounds. All four places would have to move together, and the knowledge check distractors would need re-spacing. Recommendation: leave it, and if it is ever changed use 'about 160,000 pounds a year' so the figure is not tied to one accounting basis.
findings.evidence: standard Valor Ecclesiasticus totals (Knowles); no single settled value found within the search budget

findings.claim: Within a year they had compiled a detailed record running to six volumes.
findings.truth: The six volumes are the nineteenth-century Record Commission printed edition, not the 1535 returns, which survive as rolls and books. Not worth an edit at GCSE level.
findings.evidence: general knowledge of the Valor Ecclesiasticus edition

findings.claim: It is also a uniquely detailed historical source: no other pre-modern European country produced anything comparable in the 1530s.
findings.truth: An unverifiable superlative. It costs no marks and is not obviously false, so it stays, but it is the kind of sentence that should not survive a rebuild.
findings.evidence: no source found

findings.claim: Kenilworth Castle served different functions across its 750-year occupied history, and the lesson description repeats '750 years'.
findings.truth: The lesson itself runs c.1125 to 1650, about 525 years. The 750 figure only works if occupation of Leicester's Gatehouse into the twentieth century is counted. Left alone: the lesson description is already over the 100-character limit and would need rewriting in full.
findings.evidence: internal inconsistency with the lesson's own dates

findings.claim: Henry Beighton's 1716 engraved 'prospect' of Kenilworth.
findings.truth: Beighton was a real Warwickshire engraver whose prospects were used in the 1730 edition of Dugdale, but the 1716 date could not be confirmed from the sources available in this pass. The claim is plausible and stays as it is.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Kenilworth Castle' does not mention Beighton; no other source checked

findings.claim: The First Suppression Act targeted approximately 374 houses; about 825 monastic houses held around 10,000 religious (lessons 1, 4 and 5).
findings.truth: Both are standard textbook figures with a spread in the literature (the 1536 Act covered roughly 400 houses, and estimates of religious houses run from about 800 to 900). No corrected value was established, so they stay.
findings.evidence: no settled value found within the search budget

summary: Every practice question in all ten lessons carried another board's question form, so all 60 labels and the mark schemes that named a tariff were rewritten to this paper's four forms. The Kenilworth lessons carried four hard errors: the Great Mere dated to the 1240s rather than to King John 1210-16, Henry III described as taking the castle in 1244 when he granted it to Simon de Montfort, the younger Simon said to have been defeated at Evesham and to have held the castle through the 1266 siege, and a keep wall thickness of 4.5 metres. Three items are left for Tom to rule on.
